platform: web-app (Ring Appstore partner app, opened from the Ring app's browser and on a laptop; phone width matters)
metaphor: a flood staff gauge bolted to the basement wall, read with a humidity indicator card: enamel staff with E-ticks carries time from sensor to dry; water is the indicator's pink
register: precise, calm (a homeowner at 2 a.m. and an adjuster reading later; credible, never alarming)
expressive_axis: structure: the enamel gauge staff runs through the incident and is the timeline
category_convention_avoided: Smart-home security apps and claims portals: white rounded cards, a corporate blue (Ring's own navy and blue included), stock line icons, a tidy stepper, a hero stat row. The previous Watermark build was the other default: Georgia on warm paper with hairline rules.
design_code: Time is drawn on an enamel staff with E-ticks, not listed in a table, because an adjuster's first question is how long the water stood and a gauge answers that at a glance.

There is exactly one hue, the humidity-indicator pink, and it appears only where water is confirmed (sensor faulted, a frame the caption says shows water, the fill on the staff), because colour that means 'wet' everywhere else would make the evidence argue.
Anything the system could not verify is drawn as hatching, never as a colour, because the pack's credibility rests on disclosing gaps without dramatising them.
Readouts are set in condensed industrial numerals with tabular spacing on machined, square-cornered plates, because the product is an instrument record, not a dashboard of opinions.
anti_brief: Red alarm styling or flashing: the user opens this mid-flood and an adjuster reads it later; panic colour reads as advocacy, not evidence.
Rounded cards and a blue accent: the category default, and Ring's own palette, which a partner app should not imitate.
Paper and serif documents: the attractor the previous build fell into.

axes.canvas: dark damp-concrete green-grey (home); limewashed concrete in light
axes.type_voice: condensed industrial display for readouts and labels + humanist body
axes.structure: gauge staff spine with plates hung off it; dashboard is a row of station gauges per sensor
axes.depth: dark: lighter plates step up, inset bevel line on top edge; light: 1px rule + hard 1px drop line, no blur
axes.ornament: the gauge itself: E-ticks, stage marks, hatching
axes.motion: detented: water fill rises in steps; plates snap in
axes.numerals: tabular everywhere; seconds as integers; null shown as an en-dash

tokens.wet_role: confirmed water only: faulted sensor, a frame captioned as showing water, the fill on the staff
tokens.type_display: Big Shoulders (variable, opsz axis; Google merged Big Shoulders Display into it)
tokens.motion_easing: steps(6, end) for the water fill; cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) for plates

motion_brief.explains: that water was confirmed and how far the record has run; that a new frame arrived
motion_brief.signature: the stage fill: the pink water level climbs the staff in six detented steps to the current mark
motion_brief.resting: still; the only live element is a 1px tick that advances on the staff while an incident is open

locked_inputs: Ring UX design guide behaviours (Create Account emphasis, email pre-fill, linking confirmation with devices and online state, skippable first-visit tutorial, what's wrong / why it matters / where to fix it, names never ids, subscription status pointing to Ring My Apps, in-app data deletion, WCAG 2.2 AA, 'Ring app' terminology). No visual values are mandated by Ring.
notes: Ledger check: family bans luminous-emissive (hackathon-workflow), toy-playful (moxie-library), organic-soft (nature-bingo). Mechanical-industrial last used by northbound (#2E3032, hue 48, signage) and dailies (#31363B, hue 152, follow-focus rows); canvas here is darker and green-tinted, hue 334, structure is a gauge spine. Hue 334 is near changelog-studio 338 (light press room, print-editorial) and differs on canvas, family and structure. Barlow Condensed (alprosolutions) and Public Sans (assay) avoided. No mono family.
